strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: to the authors' knowledge (and verified against the related-work discussion), no prior method uses pre-trained discrete diffusion models as training-free priors for continuous image inverse problems. This is a meaningful new direction.

The methodological construction is coherent: a variational categorical distribution over z0 optimized with a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation makes the likelihood term differentiable, and the KL decomposition (Lemma 3.2) cleanly separates prior fit from measurement consistency.

The identification of the mask-absorbing limitation (Figure 2: image structure fixed within ~10% of steps, and absorbing states preventing re-masking) is a genuinely insightful observation about why naive application of discrete diffusion guidance fails, and the star-shaped noise process is a well-motivated fix that requires no retraining of the prior.
Theoretical results (Theorem 3.1 upper bound on marginal KL, Lemma B.3 marginal correctness) are provided with full proofs in the appendix, and the derivations appear correct.

Empirical evaluation is reasonable: quantitative comparisons (LPIPS/PSNR) against four established baselines on ImageNet and FFHQ for two linear tasks, an ablation against a Markov-noise variant that directly supports the central claim about star-shaped noise, memory/runtime analysis, and a cross-domain demonstration on motion data.
Hyperparameters, schedules, and baseline configurations are documented in detail (Appendix C), supporting reproducibility; limitations are honestly stated.
weaknesses: There is a theory-to-practice gap: Theorem 3.1 bounds the KL divergence, but the algorithm minimizes each term with q(z0|zt) substituted by the unconditional prior p̃θ(z0|zt), which drops the y-conditioning; the tightness of the resulting bound and the bias introduced by Gumbel-Softmax estimates are not analyzed or empirically quantified.

Results are 'comparable' rather than superior: G2D2 does not beat DDRM/PSLD on most metrics, and baselines use different pre-trained models (the authors acknowledge this), so the comparison does not isolate the method's contribution from prior-model quality.

The evaluation is narrow: only two linear tasks (SR, Gaussian deblurring), 100 images per dataset, no variance/seed reporting, no diversity or posterior-sample analysis, and the nonlinear case (a stated motivation) is deferred to future work.

The method is heavily engineered: forget coefficient, KL-coefficient and learning-rate schedules, Gumbel temperature, task-specific hyperparameters (Table 3). Sensitivity analyses are limited to the forget coefficient (Appendix C.6), leaving robustness unclear.

Two of the main ingredients (star-shaped noise, decoupled noise annealing for inverse problems) are borrowed from Okhotin et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2024); the novelty lies mainly in porting these to discrete diffusion plus the variational relaxation, which is a solid but incremental combination.

Code is only promised for release, so reproducibility currently depends on the appendix description; the preliminary motivation (Figure 2) is a qualitative, single-prompt anecdote rather than a systematic measurement.
The motion-domain experiment is purely qualitative with no quantitative metric or baseline comparison, so it demonstrates feasibility rather than performance.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely underexplored direction: training-free use of discrete-diffusion priors (VQ-Diffusion, masked motion models) for image/motion inverse problems, where the discrete/non-differentiable generative process blocks standard gradient guidance.

The variational construction (factorized categorical relaxation with Gumbel-Softmax dequantization through the codebook and decoder) is a reasonable and clearly described mechanism for making the likelihood term differentiable w.r.t. categorical parameters.

The paper identifies a real, non-obvious pathology of mask-absorbing discrete diffusion for inverse problems (early commitment of image structure, no re-masking), supports it with an illustrative experiment (Fig. 2), and motivates the star-shaped noise process as a remedy.
A dedicated ablation (G2D2 w/ Markov noise process vs. star-shaped) quantitatively substantiates the claimed benefit of the star-shaped process (e.g., LPIPS 0.409 -> 0.349 on ImageNet SR).
Experimental details are unusually thorough: hyperparameter tables, baseline settings, and a memory/runtime comparison (Table 4) are provided.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is merely 'comparable' performance, and the quantitative results are mixed at best: on FFHQ (Table 2), G2D2 is clearly dominated by pixel-domain baselines (e.g., deblurring PSNR 26.35 vs. DDRM's 31.12; SR LPIPS 0.271 vs. DPS's 0.227), and on ImageNet it never achieves the best result in any column. Given that continuous diffusion baselines are stronger, cheaper to tune, and already established, the practical significance of the method is not demonstrated.

The 'first approach to use discrete diffusion model-based priors for solving image inverse problems' claim is overstated relative to the cited related work (Chen et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024), which the paper itself acknowledges as training-free guidance for discrete diffusion; the novelty rests on a narrow domain restriction (image inverse problems) plus the borrowed star-shaped noise idea from Okhotin et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2024).

Lemma B.3 (Property 2), which underpins the correctness of the sampling scheme, appears hand-wavy: the proof asserts that the forward transition followed by reverse transitions 'effectively collapses back' to z0' and yields a Kronecker delta (Eq. 34), but the reverse conditionals q(z_{t-1}|z_t, y) are y-conditioned and, under the variational approximation, are not exact inverses of the forward process. The proof asserts rather than establishes this inversion.

The theory-to-algorithm gap is unquantified: Theorem 3.1 gives an upper bound, but the algorithm optimizes each term greedily across steps with a mean-field factorized variational family, so the bound's tightness and the posterior-approximation quality are never evaluated; additionally, substituting p~theta(z0|zt) for q(z0|zt) (Section 3.2) is an uncontrolled approximation.

The evaluation is narrow: only 100 images per dataset, only two linear tasks (4x SR, Gaussian deblurring), no variance/confidence intervals across repeated runs, no nonlinear tasks, and no comparison against the directly relevant discrete-diffusion guidance baselines (Chen et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024), which weakens the 'first' and 'comparable' claims.

The method appears hyperparameter-heavy and fragile: task-specific eta_KL, learning rates, and logarithmic scheduling constants (Table 3), a forget coefficient, Gumbel-Softmax temperature, plus 30 Adam iterations per diffusion step, none of which are justified by ablation; this raises concerns about reproducibility and generalization to new tasks (code is only 'planned' for release).
The Gumbel-Softmax relaxation of the likelihood gradient introduces bias and temperature sensitivity that are not analyzed, even though the likelihood term is the core of the guidance mechanism.

The motivation for using discrete diffusion priors for images at all is under-argued: VQ-Diffusion is an older, weaker image prior than the continuous/LDM baselines compared against, so 'comparable' results with a weaker prior do not establish that the discrete-diffusion route is useful for images; the motion experiment is qualitative only with no quantitative metric.

strengths: Novel and practically motivated contribution: G2D2 is, to my knowledge, the first training-free gradient-based inverse problem solver that scales to large discrete diffusion priors (VQ-Diffusion) and masked generative models, addressing both the non-differentiability obstacle (Gumbel-Softmax variational relaxation) and the mask-absorbing-process limitation (star-shaped noise process with inherent re-masking).

Theoretical framework is carefully constructed: Theorem 3.1 provides an upper bound linking the marginal variational KL to per-step conditional KLs, Lemma 3.1 gives the prior/likelihood decomposition, and Lemma D.1 proves the star-decomposed distribution preserves the target marginal. Proofs in the appendix are correct and complete to my reading, and the authors are transparent that the decomposed joint differs from the true star-shaped joint (Property 3).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: two datasets (ImageNet, FFHQ; 1000 images each), two tasks (SR x4, Gaussian deblurring), multiple metric types (LPIPS, PSNR, plus SSIM/FID/KID in appendix), strong baselines (DPS, DDRM, PSLD, ReSample), and a key ablation (G2D2 w/ Markov noise process) that directly supports the central claim that re-masking is the critical ingredient (e.g., LPIPS 0.340 vs 0.442 on ImageNet SR).

Practical significance: up to 77% GPU memory reduction (4.7 GiB vs 20.9 GiB for PSLD) enabling 8 GiB consumer cards, with quantitative memory/speed comparison (Table 5). The motion experiment (path-conditioned generation with MMM) demonstrates generality of the approach to other discrete-latent domains without retraining.

Good supporting analyses: text-conditioning ablation (Table 6), prior-model ablation (Table 7), forget-coefficient study (Fig. 6), explicit failure-mode analysis (Fig. 9), closed-form cumulative transition derivation, and full hyperparameter disclosure.
Honest limitations discussion (linear problems only, sampling speed, modality extension) and an ethics statement.
weaknesses: Potential information leakage in the ImageNet experiments: G2D2 uses text prompts of the form 'a photo of [Class Name]', i.e., the ground-truth class label is supplied at inference time, while DPS appears to use an unconditional ImageNet model (only ReSample receives class labels). This conditioning could inflate G2D2's ImageNet numbers relative to baselines and complicates the 'comparable to continuous methods' claim; an unconditional-prompt comparison for the main tables would strengthen the evidence (Table 6 suggests modest but real gains from conditioning).

The algorithm is a greedy per-step procedure (sequential α_t optimization, warm-start initialization with forgetting coefficient γ, Gumbel-Softmax temperature, dynamic lr/KL schedules) that deviates from the theoretically motivated objective; the bound in Theorem 3.1 justifies the loss shape but no error analysis connects the practical algorithm to the bound, and the substitution of p̃θ(z0|zt) for q_star(z0|zt) (approximating the prior KL) introduces unquantified error.

Computational cost remains high: 194 s/image vs 4 s for DDRM (Table 5). The memory advantage is clear, but the wall-clock disadvantage should temper the practical significance claims, particularly since DDRM achieves better PSNR on deblurring.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only linear operators and two tasks; results on nonlinear inverse problems (mentioned as future work) or harder noise regimes are absent. The ImageNet FID reference set (1,000 images) is admittedly non-standard, limiting the reliability of those auxiliary metrics.

The class-name prompt effectively encodes test-time information unavailable in the standard inverse problem setting, and the FFHQ prompt choice appears suboptimal per the authors' own failure-mode analysis (bias toward adult faces), indicating sensitivity to prompt selection.

Code availability is stated but the repository URL is blank in the manuscript text (both abstract and reproducibility statement), which hampers verification at review time; reproducibility otherwise looks adequate given disclosed hyperparameters (Tables 4, 5, and appendix).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: training-free guidance for discrete diffusion / masked generative models on inverse problems, which prior work (Gruver et al., Chen et al., Li et al.) either requires additional training or does not scale to large discrete latent spaces like VQ-Diffusion.

The methodological framing is coherent and reasonably rigorous: the star-decomposed distribution (q_star-decomp) is introduced with a clear statement of its properties, Property 2 (identical marginals to the target posterior) is proved in the appendix, and the variational objective in Theorem 3.1 is derived with a complete proof, connecting prior-fit and likelihood terms in a principled way (Lemma 3.1).

The insight that mask-absorbing noise processes structurally freeze early-stage errors and that a star-shaped process provides 'inherent re-masking' is well-motivated and empirically demonstrated (Figure 2, Figure 3, and the Markov ablation in Tables 1-2, which shows large degradations without the star-shaped process). This ablation is the strongest experimental evidence in the paper.

The GPU memory claim (4.7 GiB vs 20.9 GiB for PSLD) is supported with a dedicated measurement table (Table 5) and hardware details, and the wall-clock cost of the method is honestly reported (194 s/image, slower than DDRM's 4 s).

The appendix contains useful self-critical analyses: failure modes (E.9), text-conditioning ablations (E.7), prior-model sensitivity (E.8), and explicit caveats about FID reference-set limitations. The limitations/future-work section is candid about nonlinearity and speed gaps. Ethics and reproducibility statements are present.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is questionable. G2D2 is conditioned on text prompts containing the ground-truth class name for ImageNet ('a photo of [Class Name]'), which is oracle information; baselines like DPS use unconditional pixel-domain models. While ReSample also receives class labels, the text prompt advantage is not disentangled, and the E.7 ablation shows conditioning affects ImageNet results. The paper also concedes that 'the pre-trained models used for each method are different,' which undermines the headline claim of 'comparable performance to continuous counterparts' — the comparisons partly measure prior quality rather than the guidance method.

The theoretical bound (Theorem 3.1) does not directly justify the algorithm: the bound involves expectations under the variational marginals, but the algorithm minimizes each per-time-step term independently over a sequentially sampled trajectory, so the connection between the optimization and sampling from the true posterior is loose. Additionally, substituting the learned prior for q_star(z0|zt) in Eq. (8) is an uncontrolled approximation on which the whole objective rests, and the impact of this substitution is not analyzed.

The evaluation scope is narrow: only two linear tasks (SR x4 and Gaussian deblurring), no inpainting, no nonlinear operators, and noise is fixed at sigma=0.05. The paper itself frames G2D2 as addressing linear inverse problems; broader task coverage (e.g., inpainting, where Gu et al. 2022 already provided a training-free discrete-diffusion approach) would substantially strengthen the significance claim.

On the motion task (Table 3), G2D2's trajectory and location errors (0.272, 0.116) are far worse than even the weaker baseline GMD (0.176, 0.049), despite comparing against fine-tuned methods. The 'first to accomplish this without additional training' framing does not offset the large gap in the actual controllability metrics.

Reproducibility is undermined by an incomplete code link (the abstract and reproducibility statement leave the URL blank). The method also has many scheduling and weighting hyperparameters (learning-rate and KL schedules, forget coefficient, Gumbel temperature) tuned per task/dataset, with limited sensitivity analysis beyond the forget coefficient (E.6).

The runtime cost (30 optimization steps x 100 diffusion steps, 194 s per image) is significant relative to non-gradient methods, and the paper does not report compute-equivalent comparisons against alternatives such as discrete predictor-corrector re-masking (Lezama et al., 2023; Campbell et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2024), which are cited as the natural competing way to enable re-masking but never empirically compared.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and relatively underexplored problem: training-free gradient-based guidance of pre-trained discrete diffusion models for inverse problems in continuous measurement spaces, where prior work either required additional trained guidance networks or did not scale to large discrete latent spaces (VQ-Diffusion).

The methodological design is well-motivated and clearly presented: the identification of the mask-absorbing process as a fundamental obstruction (early tokens 'frozen', demonstrated empirically in Figure 2) is a useful insight, and the star-shaped noise process provides an elegant inherent re-masking mechanism without the cost of rolling back samplers.

Theoretical treatment is reasonably careful: Theorem 3.1 provides a KL bound justifying the per-step variational objective, Lemma 3.1 gives the prior/likelihood decomposition, and Lemma D.1 proves the star-decomposed distribution preserves the target marginal q_star(z0|y), including the honest acknowledgment (Property 3) that the joint distributions differ.

The empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive: two tasks (SR, Gaussian deblurring), two datasets (ImageNet, FFHQ, 1000 images each), four strong baselines across pixel-domain, LDM, and discrete priors, an ablation isolating the star-shaped process (G2D2 w/ Markov shows clear degradation), sensitivity studies (forget coefficient, text conditioning, prior model choice), explicit failure-mode analysis (Figure 9), and memory/speed measurements showing a substantial 4.7 GiB vs 20.9 GiB advantage.

Demonstrating applicability beyond images via a training-free path-conditioned motion generation experiment on MMM, and showing G2D2 extends to masked generative models, strengthens the significance claim.
Reproducibility is adequately addressed: public code, pre-trained model links, closed-form transition matrices, full hyperparameter tables, and an explicit FID reference-set limitation disclosure.
weaknesses: Performance is comparable rather than superior to continuous-diffusion baselines: DDRM notably dominates on Gaussian deblurring (e.g., 30.89 vs 26.91 PSNR on FFHQ; 27.61 vs 23.37 on ImageNet), and DPS is better on FFHQ SR in LPIPS. The headline gains are memory footprint and training-free applicability, which is a useful but modest advantage.

The prior model used for ImageNet and FFHQ evaluation (VQ-Diffusion trained on ITHQ) is mismatched with the evaluation datasets, acknowledged by the authors themselves; this makes the 'comparable to continuous counterparts' claim harder to interpret and gives pixel-domain models trained on the target datasets an advantage that is not controlled for.

The variational objective rests on heuristic steps beyond the stated theorem: q_star(z0|zt) is substituted by the pre-trained p_tilde_theta without analysis of approximation error, and the per-step minimization ignores the coupling of all alpha's through p_alpha(z_t|y) in the bound of Theorem 3.1 — i.e., the sequential procedure is not shown to actually minimize the left-hand side. No posterior-fidelity analysis or measurement-consistency statistics are reported.

Restricted to linear inverse problems with known isotropic Gaussian noise; nonlinear tasks (phase retrieval, nonlinear blur) that DPS handles are not explored, limiting scope. The speed is also weak: 194 s/image vs 4 s for DDRM, so the practical trade-off is memory for a large time cost, which the limitations section only partially addresses.

The motion experiment is a weaker showing: trajectory (0.272 vs 0.053) and location errors are substantially worse than fine-tuned baselines OmniControl and GMD, and the claim of 'first' for discrete-latent path following is a narrow novelty claim.

A large number of hyperparameters (dynamic KL coefficient and learning-rate schedules, forget coefficient, Gumbel-Softmax temperature, task-specific bases) with limited sensitivity analysis beyond the forget coefficient raises concerns about robustness and tuning burden when transferring to new tasks.
Writing has minor issues: the abstract leaves the code URL blank, and some redundancy between Sections 3.1-3.3.
